title: Studying at the Medical University of Gdansk
paragraphs: Through the overseas clinical clerkship exchange program, I was allowed to study abroad for 11 weeks at the Medical University of Gdansk in Poland. Here I will describe what I experienced through the study abroad. First, the name Gdansk may be unfamiliar, but it is a port city in northern Poland and is actually also known as the place where the Second World War began. It is also famous in Europe as a travel destination for its beautiful scenery, and in recent years tourists from China and South Korea have been increasing (though it is still unknown in Japan...). In such a place I did clerkships at the Medical University of Gdansk hospital for about three months. First, I will describe the hospital clerkships. At the Medical University of Gdansk there is a system called the English Division, in which all classes and clerkships are conducted in English, with the aim of producing doctors who will be active in English-speaking countries in the future, and I was allowed to join that group. In the English Division students gather from countries all over the world, including Asia, so even when I took part as a Japanese person I was taken to be a local student rather than an international student. Classes and clerkships are all conducted on the same schedule and rules as local students, so while I could interact with local students, the doctors also ask relentlessly probing questions. Also, as in the fifth-year clerkships in Japan, the department rotates every week, so I could experience clerkships in quite a lot of fields. The classes themselves also differ from Japan, and what was impressive was the toxicology and emergency class. There, students alone took histories and did physical examinations of drug addicts and patients who had just attempted suicide, reported to the doctor, and checked answers about the patients with the doctor. It was extremely stimulating and impossible in Japan. In addition, in the endocrinology class, a patient was called in front of the whole class (about 40 people), and students began asking questions and guessed the disease and treatment. There were many students, and some were proactive, so questions were flying around the whole classroom. Although the classes and clerkships were quite different from Japan like this, I was able to learn a great deal by taking part. I strongly recommend the Medical University of Gdansk especially to those who want to learn across many fields in English and those who want to interact with local students.

Next, I will introduce what shocked me in terms of cultural differences. First, religion. In Poland Christianity is practised, and although young people are moving away from religion, the majority of the people are still Christians. What surprised me was that Christianity regards Sunday as a day of rest, so many shops, including supermarkets, are closed on Sundays. In Japan it is the day when shops are busiest, whereas in Poland they were not even open, which was interesting, and, not used to it, I repeatedly ran short of food on Sundays. Also, because I belonged to the English Division, which consists of students from various countries, the students' religions were also varied, and at meals there were people who could eat only halal food and people who could not eat beef. Although unrelated to religion, there were also many vegans and vegetarians among Europeans who eat no meat products at all from the viewpoint of environmental awareness. Among students we held several food parties and I joined with Japanese dishes, but every time there were many people who could not eat my Japanese dishes for some reason, and I realised that there are surprisingly few dishes that everyone in the world can eat. Even with meals alone, there were such differences in culture. Another shocking thing was mealtimes. In Poland there is no meal around 12 to 13 o'clock, which corresponds to Japanese lunch. Mealtimes are when you wake up (breakfast), around 15:00 (dinner) and, for some people, a late-night meal (supper). Because the concept of lunch at noon does not exist, the clerkship continued without a break from 12 to 13 until it ended around 15:00, and I studied with my stomach growling. In addition, I also realised differences in interest in politics. All the doctors and students had their own opinions on politics and solid grounds supporting them, and political topics were quite common. I knew it was said that young people who are not interested in politics are increasing in Japan, but going abroad I could not help realising the fact. In particular, in Poland, where war and the like are occurring nearby, the situation may be reflected and discussion was lively, but I was moved to see them think seriously about their own country and express themselves with passion. Japan, where prices keep rising but wages do not, and which may be exposed to danger amid an unstable world situation, made me feel the importance of being involved with responsibility as citizens in deciding what kind of future to make. As these examples show, things that I had come to feel were "taken for granted" while in Japan were different abroad, and I was made to feel diversity. Although it was only three months, it was an irreplaceable time that changed my view of life. I have nothing but gratitude to the professors of Nagoya University who made preparations for the study abroad, the professors of the Medical University of Gdansk who permitted me to be accepted, and the students who became my friends locally. Thank you.
